name: Third World socialism
summary: Third World socialism is the family of mid-twentieth-century, mostly non-Marxist socialisms in newly independent or developing countries, which treat socialism as the road to a strong, developed and truly independent nation. It combines state planning, nationalisation of key sectors and public responsibility for welfare with anti-imperialism, non-alignment and demands for a fairer world economy. Its governments were often led by strongmen or one-party systems, and drew on local traditions such as Ujamaa, Islam or Christian socialism.
scope: The mainstream of the 1950s-70s Afro-Asian and Arab strand as described in Wikipedia's article and documented in Nyerere's Arusha Declaration (1967), Nkrumah's Neo-Colonialism (1965), the Bandung Conference (1955) and the Non-Aligned Movement; Nasser, Nehru and Peronism appear as variants. Latin American socialism of the 21st century and Marxist-Leninist Cuba are excluded as separate or only partly overlapping strands; Marxist-leaning answers (class struggle, vanguard) are scored as split.

keyFigures.name: Julius Nyerere
keyFigures.role: Tanzania's first president and author of Ujamaa and the Arusha Declaration.

keyFigures.name: Kwame Nkrumah
keyFigures.role: Ghana's first leader, five-year-plan advocate, Non-Aligned Movement founder and theorist of neo-colonialism.

keyFigures.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser
keyFigures.role: Egyptian president who nationalised the Suez Canal and key industries and led Arab socialism.

sources.title: Non-Aligned Movement
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Non-alignment, bases, disarmament, debt and the New International Economic Order.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The core principle quoted in the Wikipedia article is that government bears direct responsibility for people's welfare, and Guevara's revolutionary medicine and Peronist welfare states put it into practice.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Not a headline demand, but the welfare-state orientation and Arusha's insistence that incomes not be grossly divergent imply support for wage floors.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Leaders nationalised major sectors and used five-year plans, and Arusha puts the main means of production under state and cooperative control rather than markets.

public-ownership.rationale: Arusha states that the major means of production and exchange (land, banks, minerals, large industry) should be controlled by the state; Nasser nationalised Suez and key industries.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Arusha opposes a class living off others' labour and grossly divergent incomes, which implies progressive taxation, though it relies more on ownership and leadership codes than taxes.

unions-good.rationale: Peronism and Nasserism built on organised labour and TANU claimed to be a party of workers and peasants, though unions were usually kept under state or party guidance.

property-fundamental.rationale: Arusha holds land belongs to the nation and warns against capitalist and feudal practices, so private property is subordinate to national development.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Nkrumah wants foreign capital to operate only within a national plan serving the host state, and states nationalised or controlled key firms and exports.

cut-welfare.rationale: The shared principle is direct government responsibility for citizens' welfare; Peronist Argentina built a welfare state.

worker-ownership.rationale: Arusha wants control by workers and peasants through government and cooperatives, but practice was state and parastatal ownership rather than firm-level worker ownership.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; strongman and one-party regimes used security powers but no doctrine on terrorism surveillance exists, so adherents are split.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the generally conservative social outlook of Arab and African socialism and state-led development discipline.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Not addressed; anti-racism is central to Bandung but speech law is not discussed.

strong-leader.rationale: Wikipedia notes many Third World socialist states were run by strongmen, big men or one-party systems, and leaders like Nasser and Perón embodied this.

state-harmful.rationale: Socialist development is carried out through the state, which Arusha makes the owner of the major means of production; state anarchism is foreign to it.

limit-guns.rationale: Not addressed; no doctrine, and revolutionary regimes such as Cuba armed militias while others restricted arms.

empower-police-military.rationale: Not addressed directly; militaries were central in Nasserism and Peronism but Nyerere-style socialism was civilian, so adherents differ.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the conservative social base (Islamic and Christian-influenced) of the major variants.

decide-locally.rationale: Planning and national unity were centralised; Nkrumah attacks fragmentation into small units and Arusha's ujamaa villages were directed from the centre.

rehabilitation.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; no adherent consensus.

traditional-family.rationale: Not stated directly; Arab socialism is described as adapted to conservative Islamic roots, and African socialism invoked the traditional extended family, so mild support is inferred.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the conservative religious and traditional outlook of the main variants and their governments.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the conservative Islamic and Catholic social context, with state-socialist exceptions such as Cuba.

more-religion-public.rationale: Arab socialism used Islamic rhetoric and Perón drew on Christian socialism, but secular leaders such as Nehru and Nkrumah differed.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Bandung affirms the equality of all races and condemns colonialism, and redress of colonial racial hierarchy is a standing aim.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Mid-century Third World socialists never took a position on gender theory, and conservative religious and traditional bases pull against it while women's rights rhetoric pulls for it.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Arab and African socialism rooted socialism in indigenous culture and traditions, and anti-colonial nationalism prized cultural authenticity.

gradual-change.rationale: Leaders pursued rapid state-led transformation and nationalisation, though most preferred reform to revolution; they do not defend inherited institutions as such.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Not addressed; a Third World concern was emigration and pan-regional unity, not immigration into poor countries.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Arusha commits to world peace through the UN, but the movement was wary of Western-dominated bodies and seeks UN reform, so mixed.

free-trade.rationale: Nkrumah describes terms of trade set by rich countries as a mechanism of neo-colonial extraction, and states favoured protection and export-control boards.

nation-first.rationale: Fierce national independence, but combined with solidarity, non-alignment, and unity; adherents reject both global governance and chauvinism.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Bandung and non-alignment stress non-interference in internal affairs and sovereignty, so intervention even on human-rights grounds is distrusted.

open-borders.rationale: Sovereignty and territorial integrity are core Bandung principles; open borders were not an aim, though pan-Africanists wanted unity across colonial borders.

limit-growth.rationale: Socialism was seen as the route to a strong developed nation, so growth was a central priority.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Era predates climate politics; inferred only that the Third World demands rich countries bear responsibility while prioritising development.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Industrialisation and modernisation were treated as the path out of underdevelopment, though Nyerere stressed agriculture and people over technology.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Not addressed; nuclear programmes were pursued by some states (India, Egypt) but opposed by others.

revolution-justified.rationale: Anti-colonial struggle and movements like Cuba's justify revolution, although Wikipedia notes most were reformist rather than revolutionary.

experts-over-public.rationale: Not addressed; technocratic planning coexisted with populist rhetoric.

central-planning.rationale: Nkrumah praised five-year plans and Perón and Nasser used them, though most states ran mixed economies, so planning rather than full command economy.

socialized-markets.rationale: Nasser's Egypt left some sectors to citizens' private investment while publicly owning key ones; mixed economies were common.

land-value-tax.rationale: Not addressed; land belongs to the nation in Arusha but a tax scheme is not discussed.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Not stated directly; inferred from opposition to grossly divergent incomes and to classes living off others' labour.

basic-income.rationale: Not addressed; welfare was via services and employment, not cash transfers.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Import-substituting industrialisation, export boards (Ghana cocoa, Argentine IAPI) and state industry are defining economic policies.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Nkrumah says foreign investment should follow a national plan drawn up by the state, and Wikipedia documents state planning and state enterprises.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Arusha places land and major means with the nation and cooperatives, not small proprietors; Nyerere collectivised villages.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Arusha speaks of fair incomes, not their abolition; mixed-economy socialists kept wages.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Perón nationalised banks and states put finance under public control.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Peronism and Nasserism organised labour and employers under state-guided bodies; plausible but not every strand.

one-party-rule.rationale: Wikipedia notes one-party systems were common (TANU, ASU, Ba'ath) but Nehru's India and others were multiparty, so adherents split.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The major regimes (Nasser's overthrow of King Farouk, republican Ba'athism) were republican and anti-feudal.

democracy-best.rationale: Arusha says true socialism cannot exist without democracy, but strongman and one-party practice shows a split.

direct-votes.rationale: Not addressed; plebiscites were used by some leaders but no doctrine.

workers-councils.rationale: Arusha places power in the party and state led by workers and peasants, not in councils replacing parliament.

right-to-secede.rationale: Nkrumah condemns Balkanisation into small states as neo-colonial and prizes national and continental unity.

natural-rulers.rationale: Arusha begins from the equality of all human beings.

political-violence-never.rationale: Armed anti-colonial and revolutionary struggle was accepted, though Nyerere and Nehru were also peace-oriented.

war-builds-character.rationale: Bandung emphasises peaceful settlement of disputes, so glorifying war is unlikely.

separate-church-state.rationale: Secular leaders (Nkrumah, Nehru) favoured separation while Arab socialism leaned on Islamic roots, so split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Arab socialism was non-Marxist but not theocratic; most regimes were secular-nationalist.

private-courts-defense.rationale: State control of the main means, including defence and public order, is basic; private provision is the opposite of the programme.

military-superiority.rationale: Non-aligned states stressed national defence but opposed arms races, so no clear commitment.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Anti-colonial states were multi-ethnic and Nkrumah wanted wider unity, though Arab nationalism was linguistic-cultural.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Non-Marxist variants like Arab socialism and Ujamaa reject class struggle, while Cuban and Marxist strands accept it.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Arusha says incomes should not be grossly divergent, yet it does not demand strict equality.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not directly addressed; land belongs to the nation, not to separate peoples.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Nkrumah describes wealth extracted from the poor world and calls for ending ongoing extraction; reparations as such are not in my sources, so mild.

civilizational-union.rationale: Pan-Arab and pan-African unity are central, but based on region and culture; religion-based union is split.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Arusha condemns exploitation and capitalist practice and stresses community and equality.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Ujamaa stresses communal duty and the leadership code, though rights are not rejected.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Arusha treats land and nature as a resource for national development and equality, with no statement on nature's own value.

limit-population.rationale: Not addressed; positions varied by country (India promoted family planning, others did not).

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Industrialisation was the aim for development.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Not addressed beyond modernisation; institutions were not seen as obstacles to be disrupted for their own sake.

human-enhancement.rationale: Anachronistic for this mid-century movement; nothing in its sources bears on bodily or mental enhancement.

algorithmic-government.rationale: The movement predates AI governance and its planning tradition is human-administered; no position can be inferred with confidence.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: A digital-age question the movement never faced; state-control instincts and anti-surveillance anti-imperialism cancel out.

restore-past-order.rationale: The movement looked to modernisation and development, though some drew on traditional communalism as a model.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Leaders called their socialism pragmatic and indigenous, yet held to commitments such as public control.

direct-action.rationale: Not addressed; mass movements and strikes used alongside state power.

means-match-ends.rationale: Not addressed directly; Arusha links democracy to socialism but leaders defended strong means.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Industrial development as a route to a strong nation is the opposite.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Planned industrialisation relies on specialisation; abolition is a utopian-communist aim.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Arusha speaks of equality and fair incomes, not distribution by need as an end state.

production-for-use.rationale: Arusha subordinates production to national welfare and rejects capitalists living off others, but profit remains in state enterprises.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Arusha speaks of exploitation of man by man as a capitalist-feudal feature, but non-Marxist strands avoid the labour theory.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Arab socialism and Ujamaa were non-Marxist and rejected class dictatorship, though Cuban strands did not.

collective-farming.rationale: Nyerere collectivised land through ujamaa, but India and Egypt chose land reform with smallholders, so split.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Nkrumah condemns imperialism and neo-colonial limited wars, but the claim about war between great powers is not stated.

taxation-theft.rationale: A socialist state financed by the nation, with the state responsible for welfare, makes the claim opposite to the programme.

harm-principle.rationale: Not addressed; strong collective and state aims point away.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Arusha centres the community, and the Ujamaa tradition values the collective.

conscription.rationale: Not addressed; some states used it and others not.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Opposite of the state-led and unity-oriented approach.

state-as-business.rationale: Government as owner and provider of welfare contrasts directly with market-style government.

positive-liberty.rationale: The core idea that government has direct responsibility for people's welfare matches material freedom, and independence was seen as meaningless without development.

media-academia-power.rationale: Nkrumah blames economic and financial control by foreign powers rather than media or universities for real power, so no clear stance.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Bandung affirms equality of all races and nations.

organic-representation.rationale: Corporatist elements existed but no declared position.

total-state.rationale: States directed economy, education and culture heavily, but typically not every area of life, and Nehruvian India did not.

national-rebirth.rationale: Independence leaders framed socialism as national revival and overcoming colonial legacy.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Bandung's principles call for respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of all nations.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Arusha names feudalistic practices as something to be eliminated, and republican regimes replaced personal lordly allegiance with party and state.

bound-labor.rationale: Arusha explicitly opposes feudalism and exploitation of one by another.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Anti-neocolonial critiques see knowledge as shaped by power, but no stated epistemic doctrine.

universal-morality.rationale: Bandung appeals to universal human rights and the UN Charter, but non-Western socialists also stressed cultural particularity, so the movement is split.

single-common-good.rationale: Ujamaa and Arusha stress the community and a common national interest above competing classes.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Arab socialism aimed at liberating Arab nations from Western domination, and Wikipedia ties its critics to Israel as a beachhead of the West; opposition is the norm for the Arab strands.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Not a theme in the sources; Arab socialism supported return of displaced Palestinians, but a general diaspora citizenship right is not stated.

revive-national-language.rationale: Not addressed; some states promoted Swahili or Arabic.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Arusha calls for control by workers and peasants but mostly through party and state.

school-vouchers.rationale: State responsibility for welfare and public education conflicts with vouchers.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: State-led development spending was favoured over austerity.

economic-freedom.rationale: Arusha rejects capitalist ownership as basis of freedom and prioritises state control.

rule-by-example.rationale: The leadership code binds leaders by personal conduct, relying on example and moral standard.

national-self-determination.rationale: Bandung condemns colonialism in all its manifestations and affirms national sovereignty and independence.

force-without-un.rationale: Bandung ties conduct to the UN Charter and non-intervention.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Not addressed; secular and religious variants coexist.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Not addressed; no immigrant welfare debate arose.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Arusha stresses work and that no one should live off another's labour, but no welfare conditionality is discussed.

class-collaboration.rationale: Non-Marxist Arab socialism and Peronism promoted class harmony within the nation rather than class war.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Cultural heritage was valued in anti-colonial nationalism.

dominated-front.rationale: Bandung brought Asian and African dominated states together against colonialism, and the non-aligned movement formalised it.

workers-nation.rationale: Peronism and Arab socialism organised workers within the nation and for national development.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Arab socialism is reported to have promoted women's rights, so mild opposition.

ban-interest.rationale: Islamic socialism strands raised it, but mainstream Third World socialism did not; state banks operated normally.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Bandung affirms racial equality and condemns racial discrimination.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Marxist strands accept, non-Marxist ones see the state as above classes.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Resource nationalisation was typical (Suez, oil), so domestic production favoured, but inferred.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Poor post-colonial states had little immigration debate; Bandung's equality of races suggests tolerance but no assimilation policy is stated.

elite-replacement.rationale: Racial conspiracy theory contradicts the stated equality of races.

proportional-representation.rationale: Arusha demands democracy led by peasants and workers but says nothing on electoral formulas.

national-mission.rationale: Bandung's non-interference principle contradicts exporting a form of government; Cuba's export of revolution is an exception.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Not addressed directly; Arab socialism advanced women's rights but did not use patriarchy theory.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Arusha's leadership code is aimed at preventing corruption and class privilege among leaders.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenics contradicts the declared equality of all human beings.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Strongman and one-party states rarely prosecuted their own security forces, yet anti-colonial rhetoric condemned imperial abuses, so no stance can be fixed.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Arusha makes the state the owner of the major means of production, the opposite of a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Bandung's final communique affirms the equality of all races, which excludes discouraging mixed marriage on racial grounds.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Arusha's first principle is that all human beings are equal.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Third World socialist states built socialism nationally; Nkrumah did seek continental unity, but not world revolution as a precondition.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Anti-colonial Arab socialism treated Israel as a Western beachhead, and anti-colonialists see settler states as colonial.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Not addressed; Nehru's India debated it, Arab states kept religious personal law.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Not addressed; Arab socialism sought to abolish discrimination by religion.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not addressed beyond Gandhian influence in India; not a general position.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Not addressed; varies across secular and Islamic variants.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Not addressed; stated only in Marxist-Leninist doctrine.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Arusha holds that government must be chosen and led by peasants and workers, and that true socialism requires democracy.

trade-surplus.rationale: Nkrumah criticises unequal terms of trade, but surplus aims are not stated.

population-transfer.rationale: Bandung calls for respect for human rights and sovereignty; forced expulsion contradicts it.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Revolutionary and anti-colonial armed struggle is accepted; absolute non-aggression is a libertarian view.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Arusha builds socialism on cooperation and equality, rejecting capitalist exploitation.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: One-party states suppressed rivals, but no declared doctrine.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Nkrumah's critique of neo-colonialism, that a state is unfree if outside powers can steer it, resembles non-domination.

separated-powers.rationale: Strongman and one-party states concentrated power; separation was not a feature.

vanguard-party.rationale: TANU as a party of workers and peasants with ideological teaching resembles a leading party, but Marxist-Leninist vanguard doctrine is not claimed.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Arusha is directed at peasants and workers and condemns exploitation of the poor.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Arusha bars leaders from owning rented houses but says nothing on tenants buying public housing.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: States often controlled strikes in the national interest, but unions also had a role.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Nkrumah locates poverty in the structures of neo-colonialism, not population.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Bandung affirms equality of races and nations; multi-ethnic anti-colonial states promoted unity.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Arusha wants leaders drawn from and selected by peasants and workers through party and election, not chance; lotteries have no tradition in the movement.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Wikipedia notes strongman and one-party rule were common, and emergency powers were routinely used against internal opponents, but no source states it as doctrine, so this is inferred.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Government responsibility for welfare and state boards for food and exports imply price controls, as under Nasser and Perón.

party-controls-media.rationale: Many regimes controlled media, but Nehru's India did not, so split.

party-commands-army.rationale: Military-led regimes (Nasser) differ from party-led ones.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Immigration into poor countries was marginal to this movement and its sources contain no citizenship-timing position.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: The leadership code bans multiple salaries and limits leaders' privileges to ordinary-worker style.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: TANU members were to accept the party's creed and be taught its ideology.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Nkrumah argues African unity is essential against Balkanisation, so pooling sovereignty regionally is favoured.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Presidential systems with strong executives were typical (Nasser, Perón).

church-by-bishops.rationale: Internal church governance is outside the movement's concerns; Peronism's Christian influence did not entail a stance on episcopacy.

clerical-rule.rationale: Arab socialism was secular-nationalist and non-clerical.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Anti-colonial nationalists support their own national state.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Regimes censored art for political reasons and conservative Islamic bases favoured moral censorship, yet no doctrine states it, so adherents are split.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Presidents-for-life emerged in some states, but Nyerere stepped down.

recall-officials.rationale: Arusha's leadership code and democracy language do not mention recall votes.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The Lusaka conference added abstention from big-power military pacts and non-aligned members oppose foreign bases.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Arusha bans leaders from owning rented houses but does not ban renting generally.

people-in-arms.rationale: Cuba and Tanzania used militias, but not generally.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Nyerere stressed agriculture and village life, but it was not framed as moral superiority.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Nkrumah and Arab nationalists sought to overcome colonial divisions.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Arusha stresses peasants and workers as leaders, but leaders themselves were educated.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Bandung affirms the equality of all races and nations.

death-penalty.rationale: Third World socialist states differed widely on executions, and the movement has no doctrine on capital punishment.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Arab socialism promoted women's rights but conservative religious bases resisted sex education, so the sources give no clear line.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from modernisation emphasis.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the conservative social base.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Pan-Arab and pan-African unity cut against narrow descent rules, yet nationalism favoured blood ties; no stated doctrine.

minority-language-support.rationale: National unity and Arabisation or Swahili promotion coexisted with Bandung equality rhetoric, so adherents are split.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Arab socialism sought to end religious discrimination, but exemptions from general law are not discussed.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Not addressed; collective emphasis suggests mild disagreement.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Non-aligned movement identifies the debt burden as an obstacle to development and demanded relief and a new economic order.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Nkrumah's central argument: nominal independence without economic control is neo-colonialism.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Arusha is silent on how constitutions should be drafted, and many regimes imposed constitutions from above.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Wikipedia notes strongman and one-party systems were common in states pursuing rapid development.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: NAM criticises declining aid and demands conditions for development, though Nkrumah and Nyerere warn dependence on aid.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The Non-Aligned Movement pushes disarmament, but India and others pursued their own deterrents, so the movement is split.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Presidential systems with plebiscites or elections were typical.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Perón and others nationalised banks and put finance under political direction.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Arab socialists demanded return of occupied land, while other strands had no stance on exchange for peace.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Arusha states land belongs to the nation and must serve all rather than a few individuals.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Not addressed; most non-aligned socialists maintained friendly ties with the USSR.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental risk regulation is anachronistic for this mid-century development-first movement.

collective-defense.rationale: NAM opposes big-power military alliances and pacts.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Territorial integrity and sovereignty are Bandung principles.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Not addressed; secular leaders did, others did not.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Leaders such as Nasser, Nkrumah and Nyerere were simultaneously party leaders and heads of state, the opposite of a ceremonial nonpartisan role.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Nkrumah condemns fragmentation and states prized unity.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Nkrumah opposes fragmentation, yet loose unions with autonomy were discussed in pan-African and pan-Arab federation talk; no stated line.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Republican, modernising regimes rejected sacral monarchy.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Arusha opposes grossly divergent incomes and a class living off others, which a flat income tax would not address.

character-from-environment.rationale: Arusha's view that social systems create exploitation and equality is achievable implies environment shapes people.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Arusha's leadership code binds leaders; strongman practice differed.

space-expansion.rationale: A matter outside the movement's agenda, which stressed basic development needs.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical mixed-government theory is not part of this movement's tradition.

leader-cult.rationale: Nasser, Perón, Nkrumah and Castro were honoured as embodiments of the nation, and the strongman pattern is noted by Wikipedia.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family law reforms were outside the sources and religious personal-status law differed by country.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist doctrine; most Third World socialists did not accept it.

land-redistribution.rationale: Land reform was common (Nasser, Nehru, Cuba) and Arusha places land under national control.

refugee-return.rationale: Arab socialism supported return of displaced Palestinians; inferred for others.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Bandung's sovereignty and territorial integrity principles oppose it, although pan-Arab claims complicate.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Arab socialism was secular and sought abolishing religious discrimination.

women-must-cover.rationale: Not addressed; Arab socialism promoted women's rights.

common-currency.rationale: Pan-African unity implies continental institutions, but currency is not stated.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-Arab and pan-African unity are main causes.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Multi-ethnic states pursued national unity, while some Arab states tolerated minority institutions; no doctrine.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Bandung affirms human rights and racial equality, but advice to persecuted minorities on emigration is not part of the movement's sources.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Marxist strands accept; non-Marxist strands such as Arab socialism with Islamic rhetoric do not.

ban-cartels.rationale: The state itself controlled major sectors, not competition law.

no-bailouts.rationale: State welfare orientation implies public rescue of key firms.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Strongman and one-party states often limited courts, but liberal-democratic judicial review is not discussed in the sources.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Arab socialism is said to have promoted women's rights, but quotas for equal representation are not documented, so adherents are left undecided here.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Arusha stresses self-reliance, but colonial-bloc autarky is not an aim.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: The NAM opposes unfair trade but developing states often fear that labour and environmental clauses will serve as protectionist barriers.

moral-incentives.rationale: The leadership code and Ujamaa ethic stress duty and service over material reward; Guevara advocated moral incentives.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Guevarist foco theory in Cuba, but most Third World socialists did not.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Arusha condemns feudalism and calls for eliminating feudal practices.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Cultural decolonisation led governments to teach national or African and Arab history at the centre of school curricula, as Arab and African socialism rooted socialism in indigenous heritage.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Bandung condemns colonialism in all its manifestations.

patriotic-education.rationale: Nation-building states taught loyalty to flag and anthem, and Wikipedia describes the goal of a strong developed nation.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Redress for racial hierarchy implies opposition to ending preferences.

public-money-creation.rationale: Nationalised banking and public control of finance.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Nkrumah argues neo-colonialism is capitalism's last stage and will eventually collapse.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Bandung condemns colonialism in all its manifestations, so cultivating influence over former imperial territory runs against the movement's stance.

delink-world-market.rationale: Nkrumah wants independence from neo-colonial control but non-alignment means cooperating with all kinds of states; split on full delinking.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Nkrumah says colonial profits funded rich countries' welfare states, but explicit claim of workers not exploited is Marxist-Leninist.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Bandung affirms the equality of all races, which conflicts with private rights to discriminate on racial grounds.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Arusha links socialism and democracy but gives no stance on entrenched rights, and regimes were usually flexible about constitutions.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Anti-colonial condemnation and Nkrumah's attack on Balkanisation imply colonial divisions lacked legitimacy.

elective-rulers.rationale: Arusha holds that government must be chosen by peasants and workers, and republican regimes replaced monarchies.

minority-veto.rationale: Collective decisions by party and nation were meant to bind everyone; a single dissenter's veto is contrary to collective socialism.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Arusha's leadership code is meant to bind leaders, but no right of subjects to remove rulers is stated.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Third World socialist systems varied between strong presidents and parliaments, with no common stance.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal welfare is absent from the movement's sources and no position can be inferred.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animal use is likewise absent from the sources; agrarian development stressed farming without a stated welfare rule.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Arusha demands duty of leaders, but rejects paternalism for equality.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Arusha demands participation of peasants and workers.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Nkrumah analyses economic domination rather than cultural pacification, though anti-imperialists decried cultural imperialism.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Nkrumah describes control through trade, finance and placed officials, not Gramscian consent, so the sources leave this open.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Nkrumah states wealth flows from the poor world to the rich and prices of raw materials are fixed by rich countries.

native-born-offices.rationale: Not covered in sources; pan-African and pan-Arab ideals pull against narrow native-born rules while nationalism favours them.

party-own-road.rationale: Third World socialism stressed indigenous roads and non-alignment, including from Moscow.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Arusha rejects reliance on foreign gifts, loans and private investment, citing 'he who pays the piper calls the tune'.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Bandung stresses territorial integrity, but Arab and other states disagreed about reclaiming territory, so no single line.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Third World socialism stressed independence from colonial rulers, but formal leadership of pre-colonial descendants over settlers differed by country.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anti-fascism was not a stated founding value for these states; Peronism itself drew on fascist-era models, so adherents are split.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Socialist states opposed equating fascism and communism.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: American history is outside the sources; inferred from the movement's anti-racist stance that slavery was central.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Decolonising stance suggests removal of colonial symbols.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Not addressed by any source on the movement, and no stance can be inferred.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Not addressed by any source on the movement; no stance can be inferred.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Third World socialisms were explicitly indigenous adaptations rather than imports; Arab socialism adapted to Islamic roots.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Nasser's officers took power, but civilian-led models like Tanzania differ.

paid-care-work.rationale: Wages for domestic labour is a later feminist demand absent from these sources.

filial-duty.rationale: Ujamaa and Arab socialism stress traditional family and communal obligation, so lifelong filial duty is an inferred mild agreement.

office-by-exam.rationale: Civil service reforms differed; some states used exams while party loyalty guided others.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Nkrumah warns of foreign control of strategic economic sectors, and states nationalised them.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Personal status law reform varied from secular Tunisia to religious law elsewhere; no common doctrine.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Arusha does not state a mandate-and-recall rule, and party discipline rather than recall governed leaders.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: State welfare principle opposes privatised pensions.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Arusha holds land belongs to the nation and citizens use it.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The sources do not discuss budget powers; regimes varied between strong executives and parliaments.

single-official-language.rationale: Some states promoted Swahili or Arabic as common language while others kept colonial or multiple languages.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Arusha says land belongs to the nation and warns against foreign domination.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Bandung affirms racial equality but legal tests of disparate impact are a later and Western debate.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Arusha's emphasis on self-reliance and hard work over wealth implies it.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Cuba exported revolution, but most others did not.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Bandung forbids interference and pressure on others.

corporate-influence.rationale: Nkrumah describes foreign corporations steering policy.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Neo-colonial control by funds and officials is the concern.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Population policy ranged from family planning in India to pronatalism elsewhere and migration is not the issue.

residents-only-property.rationale: Arusha's land-belongs-to-nation principle could support limits, but local resident restrictions are not discussed.

job-guarantee.rationale: State responsibility for welfare and Peronist and Nasserist guaranteed public employment.

democratic-peace.rationale: Bandung stresses non-interference, and many non-aligned leaders distrusted democracy-promotion; no stated view of the democratic-peace thesis.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Not addressed; state-building regimes demanded obedience.

non-intervention.rationale: Bandung's principles state no nation should interfere in another's internal affairs.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union structure is not in the sources; state-guided labour federations covered both craft and industry.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Equality and sovereignty norms oppose scapegoating.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Marriage was a state-recognised institution in every major variant and conservative religious bases support it.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Government secrecy was common in one-party states while some publish more openly, so the movement has no common line.

local-production.rationale: Self-reliance and agriculture-first, but import substitution is national not local.

informal-organisation.rationale: Arusha builds socialism through a disciplined mass party (TANU) and the state, not small informal groups.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Sovereignty stressed, but UN Charter commitments also.

religious-nation.rationale: Arab socialism sought to end discrimination by religion.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Bandung opposes pressure and domination between states.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: National unity and planning; Nkrumah opposes fragmentation.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Arusha limits ownership of major means, not personal belongings.

defeat-communism.rationale: Non-alignment means cooperation with capitalist and socialist states alike.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The shared principle is direct government responsibility for welfare, so public provision is preferred over a mix with private providers.

religion-illusion.rationale: Non-Marxist variants used religious roots and rhetoric.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Capitalism seen as imperialist and neo-colonial for the Third World.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Arab socialism promoted women's rights through state action, but the sources do not tie equality to transforming the economy.

socialized-care.rationale: Some regimes expanded state welfare and nurseries, but socialised housework is a separate Marxist-feminist aim not found in these sources.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language purism appears in some nationalisms but not as a stated element of Third World socialism.

treaties-binding.rationale: Treaties with internal nations were rarely discussed; the movement stressed sovereignty and colonial treaty rejection.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Ujamaa villages as cooperative communities; but not universal.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Non-alignment and Perón's third position seek a middle course; Wikipedia notes Arab socialism as non-Marxist.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Not stated in the sources; Arab nationalists and others differ on historical versus present-population claims.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not discussed, but the movement's affirmation of racial equality and anti-racism implies rejection; inferred only.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from conservative base and actual policies.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Wikipedia notes many strongman and one-party regimes while Nehru's India and others tolerated opposition, so adherents split.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Islamic socialism may favour it, while secular Nasserists and others do not; no common doctrine.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Bandung condemns colonialism in all its manifestations, which rejects governing colonies for the ruler's benefit.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Not addressed; Islamic socialism strand only.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Arab and African socialist regimes were secular-nationalist and themselves fought religious rebellions, so this jihadist position is foreign.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Arusha demands rule by peasants and workers and democracy.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Bandung links racial and colonial oppression, but sexism and class are not combined in its theory.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the conservative social base of the main variants.

assisted-dying.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from religious and traditional social bases and the welfare orientation.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Perón's third position claims to transcend, others not.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist concept not found in the non-Marxist mainstream of Third World socialism, so adherents are split.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Arab socialism is described as adapted to Islamic roots and uses Islamic rhetoric, so it denies Islam clashes with its values.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Arusha places authority in peasants and workers, though Islamic socialist rhetoric invokes God.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Secular regimes restricted religious dress while others did not, so adherents are split.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Not covered; a late-twentieth-century labour issue outside the movement's agenda.

social-market-economy.rationale: Mixed economies appear, but with state-led planning rather than social-market competition rules, so adherents are split.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: NAM stresses disarmament, not abolition, and defence of sovereignty.

rich-first.rationale: Arusha rejects capitalists leading development and divergent incomes.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Non-alignment is the movement's defining foreign policy.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Arusha opposes feudalistic practices, though some republics (Syria, Libya) later drifted toward dynastic succession.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Mutual credit was not a feature; Islamic socialists might favour interest-free credit but state banks were normal.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: NAM lists donor conditionality as an obstacle; Arusha rejects loans giving controllers.

property-franchise.rationale: Arusha places power with peasants and workers.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Ecofeminism is absent from these sources and no stance can be inferred.

reification.rationale: A Marxist-Hegelian concept absent from the non-Marxist mainstream.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Nkrumah describes wealthy powers steering outcomes, but press freedom critique is not in the sources.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Strongman rule used decrees often, but Arusha's leadership code is an announced rule, so adherents are split.

racial-franchise.rationale: Bandung affirms the equality of all races, ruling out restricting the vote to one racial group.

open-government-data.rationale: Not covered by the movement's sources.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Personal status law in Arab states limits interfaith marriage, yet Arab socialism sought to abolish religious discrimination, so split.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Bandung's equality principles reject targeting a religious minority; Arab socialism sought to abolish discrimination by religion.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Deliberative citizens' assemblies are a recent invention outside the movement's sources.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Islamic socialism reinterprets Islam for economics but secular strands ignore religious law, so adherents are split.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Arusha opposes classes living off others' labour.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the conservative social base of governments.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Arab socialism is a non-Marxist socialism adapted to conservative Islamic roots and Perón drew on Christian socialism, which rule out state atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Third World socialist states used the state for control and development, with no abolitionist strand.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Not addressed; one-party unity was often preferred, though some states used consociation.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The movement's shared principle is direct government responsibility for welfare, not private charity.

term-limits.rationale: Nyerere stepped down but Nasser, Nkrumah and others did not, so adherents are split.

vote-delegation.rationale: Liquid democracy is a digital-age idea absent from the sources.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: A twenty-first-century concern outside the movement's agenda.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Religious institutions' internal rules were outside the movement's scope.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Arab socialism promoted women's rights, but the conservative base resisted changes to family authority.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Not covered; low-immigration developing states had no debate.

rent-control.rationale: State protection of welfare, Nasser's rent reductions inferred.

abolish-ip.rationale: Some Third World states criticised patents on medicines but abolition is not an adherent position.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Some regimes (Egypt, Ghana Young Pioneers) had youth wings.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: NAM opposes foreign military bases and promotes disarmament.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: NAM opposes military bases in foreign countries.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Bandung stresses human rights, but formal recognition of past genocides is not covered.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Arusha says no one should live off others' labour.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Bandung's principles affirm the right of self-defence in accordance with the UN Charter.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Arab and African socialism stressed indigenous roots, but claims of ancient unbroken national continuity are not a stated doctrine.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Postmodern feminist theory is absent from the sources.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Postmodern feminist theory is absent from the sources.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Independence and revolutionary movements honoured fallen fighters as national heroes, with Cuba and Arab states notable.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Arusha frames socialism as material justice and equality rather than spiritual war, though Islamic rhetoric exists.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Diaspora homeland questions were not part of the movement's sources.

culture-before-state.rationale: Political independence and state economic control came first.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Nationalisation favoured citizens, but the stated principle was national.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Nkrumah and Arab nationalists want unity of peoples across colonial borders, but the statement concerns regional administrative merging, which is not covered.

independent-unions.rationale: Third World socialist regimes generally kept unions under party or state guidance, as in Peronist and Nasserist corporatism.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Arusha says leadership must be peasants and workers, but non-Marxist regimes were led by officers and elites.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The shared principle of government responsibility for welfare supports public control of water, health and transport.

second-chamber.rationale: Constitutional design is not in the sources, and states varied between unicameral and bicameral models.

municipal-property.rationale: Arusha places the major means under the state and cooperatives for the whole nation, not under local communities alone.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Nkrumah's unity and planning favour strong central institutions, not confederations that leave decisions to local assemblies.

family-wage.rationale: Arusha wants fair incomes for workers and no class living off others; a family wage is an inferred mild implication.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Drug regulation speed is a recent debate absent from the sources.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: A transhumanist cause absent from the sources.

anonymous-payments.rationale: State control of finance and capital movement suggests distrust of untraceable payments, but it is inferred.

online-anonymity.rationale: Strong states favoured control of information, but this digital question is not addressed.

person-over-state.rationale: Arusha holds equality of persons but community priority.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Arab socialism rooted itself in Islam and Perón in Christian socialism, suggesting some endorsement of a spiritual dimension.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Nkrumah favours strong central authority against fragmentation, so regional autonomy resting on revocable powers fits.

gm-crops.rationale: Agrarian development favoured modern technology, but GM crops are anachronistic for the movement's sources.

dense-cities.rationale: Not covered; Nyerere's village focus and industrial cities pull in different directions.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Bandung affirms equality and anti-racism rather than racial group politics, though pan-African solidarity exists.

racial-pride.rationale: Nkrumah and the anti-colonial movements asserted pride of colonised peoples against colonial racial hierarchy.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Arab nationalism defines the nation by language and history, whereas African socialism accepted colonial-era multi-lingual states.

communal-electorates.rationale: National unity and secular Arab socialism that sought to abolish religious discrimination counsel against separate electorates.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Nkrumah describes Balkanisation as a neo-colonial design.

free-public-college.rationale: Government welfare responsibility supported free education, as Nasser's Egypt made university free.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Environmental taxation is anachronistic for a development-first movement.

future-generations.rationale: Not addressed in sources; no stance can be inferred.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Not addressed; Arab socialism promoted women's rights without distinct-values theory.

arms-reduction.rationale: The NAM linked peace efforts to disarmament from its 1956 Brijuni meeting onwards.

open-diplomacy.rationale: The NAM calls for transparency and democracy in international decision-making, so open diplomacy is a mild inference.

capital-controls.rationale: Planned foreign investment under national control.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The Non-Aligned Movement campaigned in the 1970s for a New International Economic Order, citing unfair trade and debt burdens.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Post-independence governments often monopolised arms, yet Bandung and the Non-Aligned Movement backed armed liberation struggles; adherents are split.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Inferred: nation-building states relied on national armies and defended sovereignty, though the movement opposed great-power wars; not stated.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Arusha stresses worker participation and egalitarian incomes, but unions were often state-controlled; support is inferred and qualified.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Anachronistic and rarely feasible in low-income states; the welfare orientation gives no clear lean.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Inferred from state planning and the movement's critique of debt and external financial conditions; binding borrowing limits would constrain development spending.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Leaders mostly took over and repurposed the inherited state and one-party structures; Marxist-leaning smash-the-state views are a minority and scored as split.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Inferred: the strand favoured national planning and state ownership of key sectors under a common blueprint.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; development priorities and traditional communal land views pull in different directions.

sacred-nation.rationale: Socialism was framed as the road to a strong, truly independent nation, and nation-building was central; the specifically sacred wording is inferred.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Anachronistic for the period and not addressed in the sources.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Nkrumah's neo-colonialism and Balkanisation analysis describes exploitative core-periphery relations; applying it within states is inferred.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Arusha asserts that all human beings are equal and entitled to dignity and respect; the not-to-be-redesigned clause is not discussed.

public-service-media.rationale: Many such states ran state broadcasters, but the statement requires independence from government control, which these regimes often denied; split.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Variants drew on Islam, Christian socialism and secular nationalism, so adherents are split on whether religions share one truth.

farm-price-support.rationale: Inferred from the state-planning and co-operative orientation and the emphasis on agriculture in the Arusha Declaration; guaranteed prices are not stated directly.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: The Non-Aligned Movement urged disarmament but India built the bomb and many members opposed nuclear powers' monopoly, so adherents are split.

workers-own-party.rationale: Many of these states were run by one ruling party of workers and peasants, so a separate independent workers' party was not a common demand; adherents are split.

ban-fgm.rationale: Not addressed by the doctrine; inferred as split because modernising leaders and traditionalist or religious variants differed.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Inferred from the egalitarian and modernising aims of the strand; equal inheritance rights are not stated in the sources.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Not addressed; Arab and African nationalist variants held differing views on language and unity, so neutral is inferred.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: State planning and public control of key sectors imply regulation and public ownership rather than private tort remedies; inferred, not stated.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Nyerere's TANU government abolished chiefs' powers and the Arusha Declaration opposes feudal privilege, so an official lawmaking role is inferred to be rejected.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Development and industrialisation took priority and the strand did not address the trade-off, so neutral is inferred.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Not addressed; strongman and one-party regimes often favoured strict penalties but adherents are not documented as agreeing.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Not addressed; the strand stressed national unity and a national language in some states but not uniformly, so neutral is inferred.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Unions in this tradition were usually tied to the ruling party and the national plan, so adherents would not treat voluntary membership as a right; inferred from the one-party and state-planning pattern in the article.

voter-id.rationale: Electoral administration was not an issue for this movement and its governments ranged from one-party states to multiparty democracies; no shared view.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Nehru-style secularism, Nyerere's multi-faith Tanzania and the Bandung principles of equality of all religions point to equal treatment, though Arab socialist states favoured Islam; inferred.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Arusha treats democracy as inseparable from equality and the people's control of the economy, and its governments defended one-party democracy, so fair elections alone were not seen as enough.

premarital-sex.rationale: Not discussed; inferred from the generally traditional social outlook of the governments and local religious traditions they drew on.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Never addressed; inferred from the strongman and one-party governments that put order and national unity first.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Not addressed; adherents favour state-run welfare and public services over a single cash transfer, inferred from the welfare-state orientation in the article.

women-suffrage.rationale: Arusha commits to equal rights for all citizens, men and women, and the Bandung principles endorse equal rights and the UN Charter.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Not addressed directly; the movement drew on religious traditions such as Islam and Christian socialism and blamed colonialism and class, not religion, for oppression; inferred.

race-social-construct.rationale: The Bandung Conference condemned racism and affirmed the equality of all races, and Nkrumah attacked racial colonialism; the biological question itself is inferred.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Inferred from the state-led development and welfare approach and mass women's unions in several of these states; not a headline demand.

missingStatements.text: Foreign-owned companies controlling a country's natural resources and key industries should be nationalised.
missingStatements.rationale: Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal and key industries and Perón nationalised railways, ports and banks, a defining step in the documented policy of these states.

missingStatements.text: Government ministers and senior officials should be barred from holding private business interests or multiple salaries.
missingStatements.rationale: The Arusha Declaration's leadership code forbids leaders from holding company shares or directorships, drawing two salaries or owning rented houses.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to Tanzania's Arusha leadership code; the general concern is covered by political-elite-corrupt and does not separate many ideologies.

missingStatements.text: The rules of the international economy should be restructured in favour of developing countries.
missingStatements.rationale: The Non-Aligned Movement campaigned in the 1970s for a New International Economic Order, citing unfair trade and debt burdens.

notes: Variants split widely: Nehru's India and Peronism were not one-party, Nyerere and Cuba collectivised land while Nasser and Nehru redistributed to smallholders, and Arab socialism stressed Islamic roots while Nkrumah and Nehru were secular. Many social-issue answers are low-confidence inferences because the movement's sources do not discuss them.
